warmup.q: A service caches FX rates as Map<String, WeakReference<RateTable>>. Nothing else refers to the rate tables. How long does a cached table survive under normal load?
options: Until the next garbage collection that finds it
Until the map entry is removed
For the lifetime of the JVM
warmup.why: A weak reference doesn't keep its referent alive. Once only weak references point to the table, the next GC that finds it clears them, which on a busy service can be milliseconds after it was cached. "Until memory runs low" describes soft references. The map entry stays, but it holds an empty reference.

sections.h: Reachability is a ladder: strong, soft, weak, phantom
sections.html:
The garbage collector doesn't free the objects you stopped using. It frees the objects nothing can reach. It starts from the GC roots (the local variables on every live thread's stack, static fields, and references held by native code called through JNI), follows every reference, and keeps whatever it finds. Everything else is garbage.

java.lang.ref lets you point at an object without holding it as tightly. Its package docs define a ladder:

  • An object is strongly reachable if a chain of ordinary references leads to it. The GC leaves it alone.
  • It is softly reachable if the only way to it goes through a SoftReference. The GC may clear that reference when memory gets tight.
  • It is weakly reachable if the only way goes through a WeakReference. The next collection that finds it clears the reference.
  • It is phantom reachable if only a PhantomReference is left. Its get() always returns null; it only tells you the object is gone.
  • Otherwise it is unreachable, and its memory can be reused.

Each reference object can carry a ReferenceQueue. "Some time after" the GC sees the referent drop to that rung, it clears the reference and puts it on the queue. That's the spec's own wording, and it promises no deadline.

Java
ReferenceQueue<byte[]> queue = new ReferenceQueue<>();
WeakReference<byte[]> weak = new WeakReference<>(new byte[1_000], queue);
System.gc();                              // a request, fine in a demo
Reference<?> gone = queue.remove(500);    // the same weak reference, once the GC cleared it
Kotlin
val queue = ReferenceQueue<ByteArray>()
val weak = WeakReference(ByteArray(1_000), queue)
System.gc()                               // a request, fine in a demo
val gone = queue.remove(500)              // the same weak reference, once the GC cleared it

A word on System.gc(). It's a request. Its Javadoc promises nothing about how much it reclaims or when, -XX:+DisableExplicitGC turns it into a no-op, and some collectors run it concurrently. This lesson uses it only in demos, and in test helpers that keep asking until a queue delivers and give up after a timeout. Never put it in service code.

try.title: Climb down the ladder
steps: Read ReferenceLadderDemo (or the Kotlin twin). It makes four 1,000-byte arrays: one strong, one soft, one weak, one phantom. Predict which survive a System.gc() and which references land on the queue.
Run it with the command below.

code.title: ReferenceLadderDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.memory.l03; import java.lang.ref.PhantomReference; import java.lang.ref.Reference; import java.lang.ref.ReferenceQueue; import java.lang.ref.SoftReference; import java.lang.ref.WeakReference; /** One object on each rung of the reachability ladder, before and after a GC. */ public class ReferenceLadderDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { ReferenceQueue<byte[]> queue = new ReferenceQueue<>(); byte[] strong = new byte[1_000]; // a plain local: strongly reachable SoftReference<byte[]> soft = new SoftReference<>(new byte[1_000], queue); WeakReference<byte[]> weak = new WeakReference<>(new byte[1_000], queue); PhantomReference<byte[]> phantom = new PhantomReference<>(new byte[1_000], queue); System.out.printf("before GC: soft %s, weak %s, phantom.get() %s%n", soft.get() != null, weak.get() != null, phantom.get()); System.gc(); // a request; fine in a demo, never a guarantee System.out.printf("after GC: soft %s, weak %s, phantom.get() %s%n", soft.get() != null, weak.get() != null, phantom.get()); for (Reference<?> r; (r = queue.remove(500)) != null; ) { System.out.println("enqueued: " + r.getClass().getSimpleName()); } Reference.reachabilityFence(strong); // keep `strong` alive until here System.out.println("strong array still here: " + strong.length + " bytes"); } }

alt.title: ReferenceLadderDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.memory.l03 import java.lang.ref.PhantomReference import java.lang.ref.Reference import java.lang.ref.ReferenceQueue import java.lang.ref.SoftReference import java.lang.ref.WeakReference /** One object on each rung of the reachability ladder, before and after a GC. */ fun main() { val queue = ReferenceQueue<ByteArray>() val strong = ByteArray(1_000) // a plain local: strongly reachable val soft = SoftReference(ByteArray(1_000), queue) val weak = WeakReference(ByteArray(1_000), queue) val phantom = PhantomReference(ByteArray(1_000), queue) println("before GC: soft ${soft.get() != null}, weak ${weak.get() != null}, phantom.get() ${phantom.get()}") System.gc() // a request; fine in a demo, never a guarantee println("after GC: soft ${soft.get() != null}, weak ${weak.get() != null}, phantom.get() ${phantom.get()}") while (true) { val r = queue.remove(500) ?: break println("enqueued: ${r.javaClass.simpleName}") } Reference.reachabilityFence(strong) // keep `strong` alive until here println("strong array still here: ${strong.size} bytes") }

try.expect: Before the GC: soft true, weak true, phantom.get() is null (it always is). After it: soft is still true, because memory isn't tight; weak is false. The queue receives the WeakReference and the PhantomReference. The strong array is untouched.

sections.h: Soft references wait for memory pressure, with no promise of when
sections.html:
SoftReference sounds made for caches, and its Javadoc says so: "Soft references are most often used to implement memory-sensitive caches." The contract is thinner than it sounds. The JVM guarantees one thing: all soft references to softly reachable objects are cleared before it throws an OutOfMemoryError. Otherwise, in the Javadoc's words, "no constraints are placed upon the time" of clearing. HotSpot ties it to a flag, -XX:SoftRefLRUPolicyMSPerMB (default 1000), described as the "number of milliseconds per MB of free space in the heap" an unused soft referent may live.

Here's what memory pressure looks like. A 64 MB heap holds a 40 MB rate table behind a soft reference, and then the code asks for another 40 MB:

GC(5) Pause Full (G1 Compaction Pause) 42M->42M(64M) 4.230ms
GC(6) Pause Full (G1 Compaction Pause) 42M->1M(8M) 10.816ms
after a 40 MB report: rate table cached: false

G1 ran a full GC (a collection of the whole heap, with every thread stopped) that kept the soft referent and still had no room. Then it ran a second full GC that cleared the soft reference, and the allocation went through. The rate table is gone, and the next request has to reload it.

That's the trouble with soft caches in a service. They empty in bulk, at the worst moment: when the heap is nearly full and the collector is already running full GCs. Then every request that missed reloads at once, against a database that is slow for the same reason. And a heap full of soft references always looks full, so you can't size it by watching it.

Use a cache with an explicit size limit and expiry instead, and size the heap for it. Lesson 7 builds one. I'd keep soft references for data that is truly optional and cheap to rebuild, and I rarely find such data in payment code.

try.title: Squeeze a soft cache
steps: Read SoftCacheDemo. It starts a child JVM with -Xmx64m -Xlog:gc, caches 40 MB behind a soft reference, then allocates 40 MB more. Predict: does the second allocation fail?
Run it and read the GC lines between the two printouts.

code.title: SoftCacheDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.memory.l03; import workbench.memory.Jvm; import java.lang.ref.SoftReference; import java.util.List; /** A 40 MB soft-referenced "rate table" in a 64 MB heap, then another 40 MB allocation. Runs in a child JVM. */ public class SoftCacheDemo { public static void main(String[] args) { if (args.length == 0) { Jvm.run(List.of("-Xmx64m", "-Xlog:gc"), SoftCacheDemo.class.getName(), "run"); return; } SoftReference<byte[]> rates = new SoftReference<>(new byte[40 << 20]); System.out.println("rate table cached: " + (rates.get() != null)); byte[] report = new byte[40 << 20]; // only fits if the GC clears the soft reference System.out.println("after a 40 MB report: rate table cached: " + (rates.get() != null) + ", report " + report.length + " bytes"); } }

alt.title: SoftCacheDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.memory.l03 import workbench.memory.Jvm import java.lang.ref.SoftReference /** A 40 MB soft-referenced "rate table" in a 64 MB heap, then another 40 MB allocation. Runs in a child JVM. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { if (args.isEmpty()) { Jvm.run(listOf("-Xmx64m", "-Xlog:gc"), "workbench.memory.l03.SoftCacheDemoKt", "run") return } val rates = SoftReference(ByteArray(40 shl 20)) println("rate table cached: ${rates.get() != null}") val report = ByteArray(40 shl 20) // only fits if the GC clears the soft reference println("after a 40 MB report: rate table cached: ${rates.get() != null}, report ${report.size} bytes") }

try.expect: No OutOfMemoryError. Between the two printouts you'll see Pause Full (G1 Compaction Pause) 42M->42M(64M), which kept the soft referent, then a second Pause Full (G1 Compaction Pause) 42M->1M(8M), which cleared it. The last line says the rate table is no longer cached. Two full GCs to empty one cache is the cost a soft cache hides.

sections.h: Weak references let go as soon as nobody else holds on
sections.html:
A weak reference holds nothing up. Once only weak references lead to an object, the next GC that finds it clears all of them at once. In the research behind this course, a short loop of GC requests cleared a weak reference on every run, under every collector it tried.

That makes weak references wrong for caches: a weakly held value lasts until the next GC, which on a busy service is milliseconds away. It makes them right for one job: attaching data to an object whose lifetime someone else controls, without making that object live longer.

WeakHashMap is that idea as a map. The keys are weak and the values are strong. When a key becomes unreachable, its entry goes away the next time you call size(), get() or put().

Java
Map<Session, CheckoutState> checkouts = new WeakHashMap<>();
checkouts.put(session, new CheckoutState("2 items"));
session = null;                 // the session ends; after a GC, checkouts.size() is 0
Kotlin
val checkouts = WeakHashMap<Session, CheckoutState>()
checkouts[session] = CheckoutState("2 items")
// when the session becomes unreachable, the entry goes after the next GC

There's one trap, and the Javadoc warns about it: a value must not refer to its own key. If a SessionAudit value holds its Session, the map's strong value keeps the weak key alive, and the entry never goes away. The demo below fills two maps and shows one emptying and the other one stuck.

The same idea gives you a listener registry that doesn't leak. A registry that keeps listeners in a plain list keeps every listener alive, plus everything each listener refers to, until someone remembers to unregister. Hold them through WeakReference instead, and a listener whose owner is gone simply disappears. The catch is the mirror image: a lambda registered inline, with no other reference to it, disappears too, at the next GC. Whoever owns a listener must keep a reference to it. The lab builds this registry.

try.title: Watch a WeakHashMap empty, and one that doesn't
steps: Read WeakHashMapDemo. Both maps get one entry, and both keys are dropped. Only the audits value refers back to its key.
Predict both sizes, then run it.

code.title: WeakHashMapDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.memory.l03; import java.util.Map; import java.util.WeakHashMap; /** WeakHashMap drops an entry when its key is unreachable, unless the value refers to the key. */ public class WeakHashMapDemo { record Session(String id) {} record CheckoutState(String cart) {} record SessionAudit(Session session, String note) {} // refers back to its own key public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { Map<Session, CheckoutState> checkouts = new WeakHashMap<>(); Map<Session, SessionAudit> audits = new WeakHashMap<>(); Session s1 = new Session("s-1"); Session s2 = new Session("s-2"); checkouts.put(s1, new CheckoutState("2 items")); audits.put(s2, new SessionAudit(s2, "opened")); s1 = null; // the sessions end: nothing else refers to them s2 = null; for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) { System.gc(); Thread.sleep(20); } // demo only: ask for a few GCs System.out.println("checkouts left: " + checkouts.size()); // size() also removes cleared entries System.out.println("audits left: " + audits.size()); } }

alt.title: WeakHashMapDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.memory.l03 import java.util.WeakHashMap data class KSession(val id: String) data class KCheckoutState(val cart: String) data class KSessionAudit(val session: KSession, val note: String) // refers back to its own key /** WeakHashMap drops an entry when its key is unreachable, unless the value refers to the key. */ fun main() { val checkouts = WeakHashMap<KSession, KCheckoutState>() val audits = WeakHashMap<KSession, KSessionAudit>() var s1: KSession? = KSession("s-1") var s2: KSession? = KSession("s-2") checkouts[s1!!] = KCheckoutState("2 items") audits[s2!!] = KSessionAudit(s2, "opened") s1 = null // the sessions end: nothing else refers to them s2 = null repeat(5) { System.gc(); Thread.sleep(20) } // demo only: ask for a few GCs println("checkouts left: ${checkouts.size}") // size also removes cleared entries println("audits left: ${audits.size}") }

try.expect: checkouts left: 0 and audits left: 1. The audit entry's value holds its Session strongly, so the weak key never becomes weakly reachable. That entry will stay for as long as the map does.

sections.h: Cleaner is the safety net, close() is the real path
sections.html:
finalize() was the first way to run code when an object died. Java 9 deprecated it, and since JDK 18 it has been deprecated for removal (JEP 421). A finalizer can bring its object back to life, finalizers run on one JVM thread in no set order and at no set time, and an object with a finalizer needs at least two collections before its memory is freed. You can check whether your service still depends on one: start it with --finalization=disabled (JDK 18 and later), and no finalizer runs. In the demo, 1,000 finalizable objects ran 1,000 finalizers by default and 0 with the flag.

The replacement is java.lang.ref.Cleaner. You register an object with a cleaning action. When the object becomes phantom reachable, the cleaner's thread runs the action. register returns a Cleanable, and its clean() runs the action at most once and unregisters it.

Java
public final class NativeBuffer implements AutoCloseable {
    private static final Cleaner CLEANER = Cleaner.create();       // one thread for all buffers
    private final Cleaner.Cleanable cleanable;

    public NativeBuffer(NativeMemory memory, int bytes) {
        long handle = memory.allocate(bytes);
        cleanable = CLEANER.register(this, new Release(memory, handle));
    }

    private record Release(NativeMemory memory, long handle) implements Runnable {
        public void run() { memory.free(handle); }                 // no reference to the buffer
    }

    @Override public void close() { cleanable.clean(); }           // the normal path, safe to call twice
}
Kotlin
class NativeBuffer(memory: NativeMemory, bytes: Int) : AutoCloseable {
    private val cleanable: Cleaner.Cleanable

    init {
        val handle = memory.allocate(bytes)
        cleanable = CLEANER.register(this, Release(memory, handle))
    }

    // a nested class has no reference to the outer object; only an `inner` class does
    private class Release(val memory: NativeMemory, val handle: Long) : Runnable {
        override fun run() = memory.free(handle)
    }

    override fun close() = cleanable.clean()                       // the normal path, safe to call twice

    companion object { private val CLEANER: Cleaner = Cleaner.create() }
}

The rule people break: the action must not refer to the object it cleans. If it does, the object never becomes phantom reachable and the action never runs. A lambda that reads a field captures this: in () -> memory.free(handle), handle means this.handle. A non-static inner class in Java captures this too. The Cleaner Javadoc warns about both.

And the cleaner is only a safety net. It runs some time after a GC, and maybe not at all before the JVM exits. Release resources with try-with-resources (use {} in Kotlin), and let the cleaner catch the ones somebody forgot.

try.title: Switch finalization off
steps: Read FinalizerDemo. It creates 1,000 objects whose class overrides finalize(), asks for 20 GCs, and counts the finalizer calls, once with default flags and once with --finalization=disabled.
Run it. Then think of one library in your service that might still use a finalizer, and how you would test without it.

code.title: FinalizerDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.memory.l03; import workbench.memory.Jvm; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; /** 1,000 objects with a finalize() method, in two child JVMs: default, and --finalization=disabled. */ public class FinalizerDemo { static final AtomicInteger finalized = new AtomicInteger(); static class LegacyHandle { @Override @SuppressWarnings({"removal", "deprecation"}) protected void finalize() { // deprecated for removal since JDK 18 finalized.incrementAndGet(); } } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { if (args.length == 0) { System.out.println("== default flags"); Jvm.run(List.of(), FinalizerDemo.class.getName(), "run"); System.out.println("== --finalization=disabled"); Jvm.run(List.of("--finalization=disabled"), FinalizerDemo.class.getName(), "run"); return; } for (int i = 0; i < 1_000; i++) new LegacyHandle(); for (int i = 0; i < 20; i++) { System.gc(); Thread.sleep(20); } System.out.println("finalized " + finalized.get() + " of 1000"); } }

alt.title: FinalizerDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.memory.l03 import workbench.memory.Jvm import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger private val finalizedCount = AtomicInteger() class KLegacyHandle { // Kotlin has no override for finalize(): you declare it, and the JVM calls it protected fun finalize() { finalizedCount.incrementAndGet() } } /** 1,000 objects with a finalize() method, in two child JVMs: default, and --finalization=disabled. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { if (args.isEmpty()) { println("== default flags") Jvm.run(listOf(), "workbench.memory.l03.FinalizerDemoKt", "run") println("== --finalization=disabled") Jvm.run(listOf("--finalization=disabled"), "workbench.memory.l03.FinalizerDemoKt", "run") return } repeat(1_000) { KLegacyHandle() } repeat(20) { System.gc(); Thread.sleep(20) } println("finalized ${finalizedCount.get()} of 1000") }

try.expect: finalized 1000 of 1000 with default flags and finalized 0 of 1000 with --finalization=disabled. The objects were still collected in the second run; only the finalizers were skipped. Running your test suite with that flag shows whether anything depends on them.

refs.title: Cleaner source at jdk-25-ga: the rules for cleaning actions

analogy: Think of the heap as a hotel. A strong reference is a guest with a booking: nobody touches the room. A soft reference is luggage in the storage room, kept until the room is full, then cleared all at once. A weak reference is a coat left in the lobby: it goes at the next sweep, however soon that is. A phantom reference is the checkout slip the front desk gets after a guest has left, so housekeeping knows to clean the room; the slip never lets you talk to the guest. Where it breaks: a hotel sweeps on a schedule. The GC sweeps when it needs memory, so you can't plan around when it comes.
world: Payment services touch native resources more than you'd think: the bank's HSM client hands out session handles, a compression codec holds native buffers, Netty pools direct memory. Wrap each in a class that implements AutoCloseable, release it with try-with-resources, and register a Cleaner only as a safety net that logs a warning when it fires, because a cleaner that fires means some code path forgot to close. A fraud-rule engine that loads and unloads rules at runtime is the classic place for a weak listener registry. And a rates cache behind SoftReference is the classic place for a pager alert: it empties exactly when the heap is under the most pressure.
mistake: Using weak or soft references as a cache. Weak values are gone at the next GC, so the hit rate falls apart under load. Soft values stay until the heap is nearly full, so the heap always looks full, and then they're cleared in bulk during full GCs, which sends a wave of reloads to the database at the worst moment. People reach for them because "the GC manages the memory for me" sounds safer than choosing a size. The fix is to choose the size: a cache with a maximum number of entries and an expiry time, and a heap sized to hold it.

compare.title: Who holds a reference to the outer object

java.title: Exporter.java
java.html: class Exporter { private final Path tempFile; // inner (the default in Java): holds Exporter.this class Cleanup implements Runnable { public void run() { deleteQuietly(tempFile); } } // static nested: holds only what you pass in static class SafeCleanup implements Runnable { private final Path file; SafeCleanup(Path file) { this.file = file; } public void run() { deleteQuietly(file); } } }

kotlin.title: Exporter.kt
kotlin.html: class Exporter(private val tempFile: Path) { // inner (you must ask for it in Kotlin): holds this@Exporter inner class Cleanup : Runnable { override fun run() = deleteQuietly(tempFile) } // nested (the default in Kotlin): holds only what you pass in class SafeCleanup(private val file: Path) : Runnable { override fun run() = deleteQuietly(file) } }

compare.note: The defaults are opposite. A class declared inside a class is inner in Java unless you write static, and nested in Kotlin unless you write inner. So a Java cleaning action written as a plain inner class silently holds the object it should clean, while the same code in Kotlin doesn't. Lambdas behave the same in both: one that reads a property or field captures this. Kotlin also has no override for finalize(): to write one you declare protected fun finalize(), which is one more reason not to.

worked.title: Find why a WeakHashMap keeps growing

steps.say: A payment gateway keeps statistics per open TCP connection to the card network. It uses a WeakHashMap so that closed connections drop out by themselves. After a day the map holds 2 million entries. Read the code and look for a strong path back to the key.
steps.code: record ConnectionStats(NetworkConnection connection, AtomicLong authorizations) {} static final Map<NetworkConnection, ConnectionStats> STATS = new WeakHashMap<>(); static void recordAuthorization(NetworkConnection c) { STATS.computeIfAbsent(c, k -> new ConnectionStats(k, new AtomicLong())) .authorizations().incrementAndGet(); }

alt.html: data class ConnectionStats(val connection: NetworkConnection, val authorizations: AtomicLong) val STATS: MutableMap<NetworkConnection, ConnectionStats> = WeakHashMap() fun recordAuthorization(c: NetworkConnection) { STATS.computeIfAbsent(c) { k -> ConnectionStats(k, AtomicLong()) } .authorizations.incrementAndGet() }

steps.say: Follow the references from a GC root. The static field holds the map, the map holds its entries, and each entry holds its value strongly. The value holds the connection. So every closed connection is still strongly reachable from STATS, through its own stats object, and its weak key is never cleared.
steps.code:
static STATS -> WeakHashMap -> Entry (weak key, STRONG value)
                                   -> ConnectionStats -> connection   <- the key itself

steps.say: Break the strong path. The stats only need something to print in logs, so store the connection's id instead of the connection.
steps.code: record ConnectionStats(String connectionId, AtomicLong authorizations) {} // no path back to the key STATS.computeIfAbsent(c, k -> new ConnectionStats(k.id(), new AtomicLong()));

alt.html: data class ConnectionStats(val connectionId: String, val authorizations: AtomicLong) // no path back to the key STATS.computeIfAbsent(c) { k -> ConnectionStats(k.id, AtomicLong()) }

steps.say: Prove it with a test that doesn't trust timing: drop the connection, keep a weak probe with its own queue, ask for GCs until the probe arrives (with a limit), then check the map. size() removes cleared entries before it counts.
steps.code: NetworkConnection c = openTestConnection(); recordAuthorization(c); ReferenceQueue<Object> q = new ReferenceQueue<>(); WeakReference<Object> probe = new WeakReference<>(c, q); c = null; Reference<?> seen = null; for (int i = 0; i < 50 && seen == null; i++) { System.gc(); seen = q.remove(50); } // bounded wait assertThat(seen).isSameAs(probe); assertThat(STATS).isEmpty();

alt.html: var c: NetworkConnection? = openTestConnection() recordAuthorization(c!!) val q = ReferenceQueue<Any>() val probe = WeakReference<Any>(c, q) c = null var seen: Reference<*>? = null for (i in 0 until 50) { System.gc(); seen = q.remove(50); if (seen != null) break } // bounded wait assertThat(seen).isSameAs(probe) assertThat(STATS).isEmpty()

lab.title: A Cleaner that runs, and a registry that forgets
steps: Run the tests. Four of seven fail; the GC waits make the failing run take about ten seconds. NativeMemory stands in for a native library: read it, but don't change it.
Fix NativeBuffer.close(): keep the Cleaner.Cleanable that register returns and call its clean(). A second close then does nothing.

Find out why a forgotten buffer is never cleaned. Look hard at the lambda: what does handle mean inside it? Replace it with a static nested class or a record that holds only the NativeMemory and the handle value.
Make WeakListenerRegistry hold WeakReference<L>. size() drops cleared references before counting. fire() drops them too, and holds a strong reference to each listener while it calls it.
Run the tests until all seven pass, then twice more.
hints: A field read inside a lambda is this.field, so the lambda captures this. Copying the field to a local variable first would also work, but a small static class makes the rule visible to the next reader.
list.removeIf(ref -> ref.get() == null) drops the cleared references.
The tests never assume a GC happened. They ask for one up to 50 times and wait on a ReferenceQueue or a condition, so a correct solution passes in well under a second.
Reference.reachabilityFence(rule) in a test keeps rule strongly reachable until that line, even if the JIT sees no later use of the variable.
lab.done: All 7 tests in ReachabilityTest pass, three runs in a row.

drill.title: Write a Cleaner-backed temp file from memory
drill.prompt: Close the page. Write a class TempExport that creates a temp file in its constructor, deletes it in close(), and deletes it from a Cleaner if nobody closes it. close() must be safe to call twice. Check your cleaning action: what does it refer to?

answer.html: final class TempExport implements AutoCloseable { private static final Cleaner CLEANER = Cleaner.create(); private final Path file; private final Cleaner.Cleanable cleanable; TempExport() throws IOException { file = Files.createTempFile("export-", ".csv"); cleanable = CLEANER.register(this, new Delete(file)); // Delete holds the path, not this } private record Delete(Path file) implements Runnable { public void run() { try { Files.deleteIfExists(file); } catch (IOException ignored) { } } } Path file() { return file; } @Override public void close() { cleanable.clean(); } // at most once }

alt.html: class TempExport : AutoCloseable { val file: Path = Files.createTempFile("export-", ".csv") private val cleanable = CLEANER.register(this, Delete(file)) // Delete holds the path, not this private class Delete(private val file: Path) : Runnable { // nested, not inner override fun run() { try { Files.deleteIfExists(file) } catch (ignored: IOException) { } } } override fun close() = cleanable.clean() // at most once companion object { private val CLEANER: Cleaner = Cleaner.create() } }

recap: The GC keeps what it can reach from the roots (thread stacks, statics, native references) and frees the rest. Reference objects add weaker rungs: soft, weak, phantom.
Soft references are cleared before an OutOfMemoryError and at no promised time otherwise. They empty in bulk under pressure, so they make poor service caches.
Weak references are cleared by the next GC that finds their referent. Use them to attach data to objects you don't own (WeakHashMap, listener registries), never for caches.
A WeakHashMap value that refers to its own key keeps the entry forever.
Cleaner replaces finalize(), which is deprecated for removal. The cleaning action must not refer to the object it cleans, and close() should call cleanable.clean().
System.gc() is a request. Use it in demos and in bounded test helpers that wait on a ReferenceQueue, never in service code.

explain.prompt: A teammate wants to free a native HSM session handle in finalize() "in case someone forgets to close it". Explain what you would do instead, and the one rule that makes it work.
explain.answer: finalize() is deprecated for removal, runs on one thread at no set time, and can even be switched off with --finalization=disabled. Make the class AutoCloseable and close it with try-with-resources, so the handle is released at a known point. As a safety net, register the object with a shared Cleaner and keep the Cleanable; close() calls cleanable.clean(), which runs the action at most once. The rule: the cleaning action must not refer to the object. Put the handle in a small static class or record, not in a lambda that reads a field, or the object can never become phantom reachable and the action never runs. If the cleaner ever fires, log it, because it means a code path forgot to close.

deeper.html:
There's a race the Cleaner pattern can hit even when you follow the rule. The JVM may decide an object is unreachable earlier than the source suggests, even while one of its methods is still running. The Reference.reachabilityFence Javadoc describes it: the JIT can load a field's value early, the object is then no longer needed, and the cleanup thread can free a resource that the method is about to use.

So a method that passes a native handle to native code should keep its object reachable until the call returns:

Java
public int compress(byte[] input) {
    try {
        return Codec.compress(handle, input);      // native call that uses the handle
    } finally {
        Reference.reachabilityFence(this);         // `this` stays reachable until here
    }
}
Kotlin
fun compress(input: ByteArray): Int {
    try {
        return Codec.compress(handle, input)       // native call that uses the handle
    } finally {
        Reference.reachabilityFence(this)          // `this` stays reachable until here
    }
}

The lab's tests use the same method for the opposite reason: to keep a listener strongly reachable until the asserts are done. Its Javadoc also states a guarantee in the terms of the memory model track: actions in a thread before reachabilityFence(x) happen-before the garbage collector clears any reference to x, so a cleanup thread sees everything the method wrote.

Two more details are useful. Phantom references used to keep their referent in memory until you cleared them; since JDK 9 the GC clears them automatically when it enqueues them, which is why Cleaner works without extra steps. And a Cleaner owns a daemon thread, so create one per library (a static final field), never one per object.
